basics/docker_basics.html:
Docker Fundamentals

A technical guide to Namespaces, Cgroups, and UnionFS

1. What is Docker?

Docker is a tool that allows you to package an application and its dependencies into a container. Unlike a Virtual Machine, a container does not bundle a full Operating System. Instead, it uses Linux Kernel features to isolate processes from the host system.

2. Linux Namespaces (The Walls)

Namespaces provide isolation by partitioning kernel resources. They create "Filtered Perspectives," where a process believes it has its own private instance of the OS.

  • PID Namespace: Allows a process to have PID 1 inside the container. It cannot see or interact with processes in other namespaces.
  • NET Namespace: Provides a private network stack, including its own IP addresses, routing tables, and firewall rules.
  • MNT Namespace: Isolates mount points, so the container sees a different root (/) filesystem than the host.
  • UTS Namespace: Allows the container to have its own hostname and domain name.
  • USER Namespace: Maps a root user inside the container to a non-privileged user on the host for security.

Technical Implementation: Namespaces are created using the clone() or unshare() system calls with specific flags like CLONE_NEWPID.

3. Control Groups / cgroups (The Rules)

While Namespaces handle what a process can see, Cgroups handle what a process can use. They prevent a single container from consuming all host resources.

  • Resource Limits: Setting maximum thresholds for RAM (e.g., 512MB) and CPU usage.
  • Prioritization: Assigning more CPU "shares" to specific containers.
  • Control: Freezing or restarting groups of processes.

4. UnionFS (The Filesystem)

Union File System is a service that "stacks" multiple directories (branches) to make them appear as one merged directory.

Key Mechanisms:

  • Layering: Docker images are made of read-only layers. These layers are shared across containers to save space.
  • Priority Rule: When two layers contain the same file, the file in the higher-priority (top) layer "shadows" the one below.
  • Copy-on-Write (CoW): If a process tries to modify a read-only file, the Kernel copies it to the top writable layer first. The original remains unchanged.
  • Whiteouts: To "delete" a file from a read-only lower layer, the system creates a "whiteout" file in the writable layer that hides the lower file from the merged view.

5. Comparison: School Setup vs. Docker

Your current environment (at school) uses Standard Permissions. You share the same Namespace, so you can see other users' folders in /home, but "Permission Denied" stops you from entering.

Docker goes further: It uses Namespaces so you cannot even see that other users exist, and UnionFS so that if you "delete" a system file, you only affect your own private "top layer" without touching the actual system.

Summary Checklist

1. Namespaces  -> Isolation (Walls)
2. Cgroups     -> Restriction (Resource limits)
3. UnionFS     -> Efficiency (Layered Filesystem)
4. Capabilities-> Security (Stripping Root powers)

basics/vm_vs_docker_tech.html:
Infrastructure Architecture: VM vs Containers

Low-level analysis of virtualization levels and resource management.

1. Virtual Machines (Hardware Virtualization)

Virtual Machines operate by abstracting the physical hardware. This is achieved via a Hypervisor (e.g., KVM, Xen, VMware).

  • Full Stack: Each VM includes a complete Guest Operating System, including its own Kernel, device drivers, and network stack.
  • Isolation Boundary: Isolation occurs at the hardware level. The Hypervisor partitions physical CPU and RAM, creating a security boundary that is difficult to breach.
  • Resource Overhead: Because each VM runs a full OS, significant RAM and CPU are consumed by the Guest Kernel and system background processes before the application even starts.

2. Containers (OS-level Virtualization)

Containers abstract the Operating System User Space. They leverage the Host OS Kernel rather than hardware virtualization.

  • Shared Kernel: All containers running on a host share the same Linux Kernel. This eliminates the need for a Guest OS.
  • Isolation Mechanism: Uses Namespaces (for visibility) and Cgroups (for resource allocation). It is a logical isolation of processes rather than physical hardware partitioning.
  • Efficiency: Since they lack a Guest OS, containers boot in milliseconds and have negligible performance overhead compared to native processes.

3. Comparative Technical Analysis

Feature Virtual Machines (VM) Containers (Docker)
Abstraction Physical Hardware Operating System (Kernel)
Guest OS Full OS required per VM No Guest OS (Shares Host Kernel)
Isolation Hardware-level (High Security) Process-level (Software Isolation)
Boot Time Minutes (Full OS boot cycle) Milliseconds (Process start)
Resource Usage Static (Pre-allocated RAM/Disk) Dynamic (Scales with usage)
Storage Large (GBs per VM) Small (MBs per Image Layer)

4. Core Logic Summary

VM Architecture

[ Application ]
[ Libs/Bins   ]
[ Guest OS    ] (Includes Kernel)
[ Hypervisor  ]
[ Physical HW ]

Container Architecture

[ Application ]
[ Libs/Bins   ]
[ Container Runtime ]
[ Host OS Kernel ]
[ Physical HW ]

5. Advanced Resource Management

In a VM environment, if you allocate 8GB of RAM to a VM, those 8GB are locked to that VM regardless of actual usage. In a Container environment, resources are governed by the Kernel's Cgroups. This allows for 'bursting' where containers can use available host resources dynamically, resulting in much higher density (running more applications on the same hardware).

srcs/docker-compose.yml:
services:
  mariadb:
    build: ./requirements/mariadb
    image: mariadb           
    container_name: mariadb
    restart: always
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/mysql
    networks:
      - inception
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mariadb-admin", "ping", "-h", "localhost", "-u", "root", "-p${SQL_ROOT_PWD}"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
  redis:
    build: ./requirements/redis
    image: redis
    container_name: redis
    restart: always
    networks:
      - inception
    command: ["--requirepass", "${REDIS_PWD}"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "-a", "${REDIS_PWD}", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
  wordpress:
    build: ./requirements/wordpress
    image: wordpress        
    container_name: wordpress
    restart: always
    env_file: .env
    depends_on:
      mariadb:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    healthcheck:
      test : ["CMD-SHELL",  "nc -z 127.0.0.1 9000 || exit 1"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s
    volumes:
      - wp-data:/var/www/html
    networks:
      - inception

  adminer:
    build: ./requirements/adminer
    image: adminer
    container_name: adminer
    restart: always
    depends_on:
      mariadb:
        condition: service_healthy
    networks:
      - inception
  nginx:
    build: ./requirements/nginx
    image: nginx            
    container_name: nginx
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "443:443"            
    depends_on:
      wordpress:
        condition: service_healthy

    volumes:
      - wp-data:/var/www/html
    networks:
      - inception
  ftp:
    build: ./requirements/ftp
    image: ftp
    container_name: ftp
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "21:21"
      - "50000-50100:50000-50100"
    volumes:
      - wp-data:/var/www/html
    env_file: .env
  website:
    build: ./requirements/website
    image: website
    container_name: website
    restart: always
    networks:
      - inception
  portainer:
    build: ./requirements/portainer
    image: portainer
    container_name: portainer
    restart: always
    ports:
      - "9443:9443"
    volumes:
      - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock
      - portainer-data:/data
    networks:
      - inception  
networks:
  inception:

volumes:
  db-data:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:
      type: none
      o: bind
      device: /home/oben-jha/data/mariadb  
  wp-data:
    driver: local
    driver_opts:

  portainer-data:

    driver_opts:

srcs/requirements/wordpress/Dockerfile:
FROM debian:bookworm

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y \
	php-mysql \
	php8.2-fpm \
	mariadb-client \
	wget \
	curl
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y netcat-openbsd && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

RUN wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wp-cli/builds/gh-pages/phar/wp-cli.phar \
	&& chmod +x wp-cli.phar \
	&& mv wp-cli.phar /usr/local/bin/wp
RUN mkdir -p /run/php
RUN sed -i 's|listen = /run/php/php8.2-fpm.sock|listen = 9000|' /etc/php/8.2/fpm/pool.d/www.conf

WORKDIR /var/www/html

COPY ./tools/auto_config.sh /usr/local/bin/auto_config.sh
RUN chmod +x /usr/local/bin/auto_config.sh


EXPOSE 9000
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/auto_config.sh"]
srcs/requirements/wordpress/tools/auto_c:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
if [ ! -f /var/www/html/wp-load.php ]; then
    wp core download --allow-root
fi

if [ ! -f /var/www/html/wp-config.php ]; then
    wp config create --allow-root \
        --dbname="$SQL_DB" \
        --dbuser="$SQL_USR" \
        --dbpass="$SQL_PWD" \
        --dbhost="mariadb:3306"
fi

if ! wp core is-installed --allow-root; then
    wp core install --allow-root \
        --url="$DOMAIN_NAME" \
        --title="Inception" \
        --admin_user="$WP_ADMIN_USR" \
        --admin_password="$WP_ADMIN_PWD" \
        --admin_email="$WP_ADMIN_EMAIL"
fi

if ! wp user get "$WP_USER" --allow-root >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    wp user create --allow-root \
        $WP_USR $WP_EMAIL \
        --user_pass=$WP_PWD \
        --role=author
fi

if ! wp config get WP_REDIS_HOST --allow-root >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    wp config set WP_REDIS_HOST redis --allow-root
    wp config set WP_REDIS_PORT 6379 --raw --allow-root
    wp config set WP_CACHE_KEY_SALT "$DOMAIN_NAME" --allow-root
    wp config set WP_CACHE true --raw --allow-root
    wp config set WP_REDIS_PASSWORD "$REDIS_PWD" --allow-root
    
    wp plugin install redis-cache --activate --allow-root
    wp redis enable --allow-root
fi

exec /usr/sbin/php-fpm8.2 -F

    apt-get install -y proftpd-core

COPY conf/proftpd.conf /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf

srcs/requirements/ftp/tools/script.sh:
#!/bin/sh
set -e

USER_CLEAN=$(echo "$FTP_USER" | tr -d '\r')
PWD_CLEAN=$(echo "$FTP_PWD" | tr -d '\r')


mkdir -p /var/www/html

if ! id "$USER_CLEAN" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    useradd -m -d /var/www/html -s /bin/bash "$USER_CLEAN"
fi

echo "${USER_CLEAN}:${PWD_CLEAN}" | chpasswd

chown -R "$USER_CLEAN":"$USER_CLEAN" /var/www/html


exec proftpd -n -c /etc/proftpd/proftpd.conf
srcs/requirements/ftp/conf/proftpd.conf:
ServerName          "Inception FTP Server"
ServerType          standalone
DefaultServer       on

# Standard FTP Port
Port                21

# Passive mode configuration
PassivePorts        50000 50100
MasqueradeAddress   oben-jha.42.fr

# Disable IPv6
UseIPv6             off

# Base permissions
Umask               022

# Number of allowed connections
MaxInstances        30

# The user/group ProFTPD runs as by default
User                proftpd
Group               nogroup

# Lock the user into the WordPress directory
DefaultRoot         /var/www/html

# Allow overwriting files
AllowOverwrite      yes

# Don't require a valid shell to log in
RequireValidShell   no

# Block anonymous login completely
<Anonymous ~ftp>
  DenyAll
</Anonymous>
